To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the market data which are necessary for the existence of an equilibrium in an exchange environment are (1) the current price, (2) the trader's own trade, and (3) the trader's trade history, which includes all past trades and the past price history.

the market data which permit the existence of rational expectations equilibria are the data which are admissible, in the sense that if a trader knows them he can determine the equilibrium price and the equilibrium volume of his own trade.
the existence of an equilibrium requires the traders to observe at least their own trade, and the equilibrium price.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what market data are necessary to permit the existence and rationality of traders’ expectations.
the following question: If traders observe some market data and form their expectations based on these data, will there exist an equilibrium in which these expectations are rational?
the following question: what market data must be observed by traders in order to permit the general existence (under reasonable conditions) of (rational expectations) equilibria?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the market data must include the equilibrium price and the equilibrium trade of the trader.
, for the general case, only the market data consisting of the equilibrium price and the equilibrium trade for each trader are admissible.
a trader must observe the equilibrium price, his own equilibrium trade, and no other data, if he is to have expectations equilibria in stochastic exchange.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the market data must contain all the information necessary to determine the equilibrium trade, and that this information must be available at all points of time.
a trader must observe his own trade and the market price in order to have expectations equilibria.

the equilibrium price, volume of trade, and the identity of the traders are the minimal set of market data which must be observed by a trader if he is to condition his expectations on the market data and have the general existence of rational expectations equilibria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order for a market to be well behaved, the traders must observe and condition their expectations on a sufficient number of market data.
the market data which traders must observe in order to support an equilibrium is the minimal data necessary to support the equilibrium.
the existence of a rational expectations equilibrium is a very fragile property of an economy, in that it is very sensitive to the market data which traders observe.
